summary: Specifies the format of ARPA Internet text messages, such as headers and addressing. It revises RFC 733 and removes features that did not gain acceptance. Replaced by RFC 2822.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 822 specifies the format of text messages passed between mail hosts. It defines how headers and addresses are written, how long headers continue across lines, and where the message body begins.

questions: what does an email header look like
what does an email header contain
subtitle: The message-content format defined for ARPA Internet text mail, including headers, addresses, dates, and body separation.

tldr.problem: Mail systems needed an agreed format for the text of messages exchanged between hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines header fields, a blank-line separator, message-body rules, and syntax for addresses, dates, and other structured fields.
tldr.outcome: RFC 822 revised RFC 733 but has since been obsoleted by RFC 2822 and updated by other RFCs listed in the unit metadata.

today: RFC 822 is an Internet Standard, but it has been obsoleted by RFC 2822 and updated by RFC 1123, RFC 1138, RFC 1148, RFC 1327, and RFC 2156. RFC 2822 is the listed replacement.

sections.title: Scope of the Message Format
sections.content:
RFC 822 defines a syntax for text messages exchanged between computer users through electronic mail. It revises RFC 733. The document treats a message as an envelope containing delivery information and contents containing the material delivered; it specifies only the contents.

The format applies to content passed between hosts. It does not dictate a site's internal storage format, the features its mail system must support, or the behavior of programs that create and read messages. The header rules are separated from rules for individual fields so simple parsers can identify fields without interpreting every field's contents.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes the message content exchanged between hosts, not the delivery envelope or a mail program's interface. Its general format lets software locate headers before interpreting their values.

sections.title: Headers, Folding, and the Message Body
sections.content:
A message contains header fields and may contain a body. The body is a sequence of text lines and begins after a null line, meaning a line with nothing before its CRLF. A header field consists of a field name, a colon, and a field body.

A long field may be folded onto multiple physical lines. A continuation line begins with at least one space or tab; unfolding treats the CRLF and following white space as white space within one logical field. Fields such as Subject may contain plain text, while address and date fields have structured syntax. Structured fields use tokens such as atoms, quoted strings, domain literals, comments, and special characters.

Comments in parentheses can nest and are ignored for formal field meaning. A backslash can quote characters only within quoted strings, domain literals, and comments, not within atoms. Most field names are case-insensitive, while text and address local parts preserve case except for the reserved name Postmaster.
sections.plainLanguage: A header can span several lines, but a space or tab marks each continuation. The software joins those lines before reading the field's value.

sections.title: Common Header Fields
sections.content:
Header fields can appear in any order except that the body follows all headers. RFC 822 recommends an order beginning with Return-Path, Received, Date, From, and Subject. The syntax requires a date, an originator, and at least one destination field; most fields may occur more than once, though the interpretation of repetitions is generally unspecified.

Received fields are added by relays to record handling information. From identifies the person or people who wanted the message sent, while Sender identifies the agent that sent it and is required when that agent differs. Reply-To directs replies; automated replies use it instead of From when it is present. To, cc, and bcc identify primary, secondary, and additional recipients.

Fields such as Message-ID, In-Reply-To, References, Keywords, Subject, and Comments identify or describe messages. A field beginning with Resent- carries information added by a forwarder. The Encrypted field can identify encryption applied to the body; headers remain unencrypted so mail transport can read them.
sections.plainLanguage: Headers identify when a message was created, who sent it, who should receive it, and how it relates to other messages. Forwarded messages can include a separate set of fields beginning with Resent-.

sections.title: Email Addresses and the Postmaster Address
sections.content:
An address is either a mailbox or a named group of mailboxes. A mailbox commonly has the form local-part@domain, optionally with a display phrase before it. The local part is interpreted by the final domain; the domain is a hierarchical name, with the top-level part at the right. This naming hierarchy is logical and does not have to describe the route a message takes.

The RFC permits abbreviated domains only within a sender's own subdomain under specified conditions; addresses must be fully specified when a message crosses a domain boundary. A domain literal can name a host using a numeric address, but the RFC strongly discourages it. Explicit source routes are also discouraged, since the mail transport service should normally choose the route.

The local part Postmaster is reserved. Postmaster@domain MUST be valid at each site and is routed to someone responsible for the site's mail system or general operation. It must be accepted without regard to alphabetic case.
sections.plainLanguage: An email address names a mailbox within a domain. Every site must accept mail addressed to Postmaster for help with its mail system.

sections.title: Revision and Replacement
sections.content:
RFC 822 revised RFC 733 by simplifying and clarifying the message format. It added trace fields such as Return-Path and Received, the Resent- forwarding prefix, and the Encrypted field. It changed address syntax to use a global address with one at-sign and a separate optional route construct.

The revision also introduced logical hierarchical domains, domain literals, named non-nested groups, a reserved Postmaster local part, and simplified date and time rules. The unit metadata records that RFC 822 was later obsoleted by RFC 2822 and updated by RFCs 1123, 1138, 1148, 1327, and 2156.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition changed the earlier rules for addresses, forwarding, tracing, and dates. Later RFCs replaced and updated RFC 822, as recorded in the document metadata.

references.text: Crocker, D.H., Vittal, J.J., Pogran, K.T., Henderson, D.A., "Standard for the Format of ARPA Network Text Message", RFC 733, November 1977.
